new_statements.quote: Since Larantuka Malay did not lose schwa sounds as did other contact varieties of Malay in eastern Indonesia, phonemic stress has not developed. Stress is regular, and is found on the penultimate syllable (Kumanireng 1993: 66).

new_statements.locator: Sec. 4.3.2.6 'Other Phonological Developments in Larantuka Malay', p. 105 (p. 129); repeated verbatim in Appendix A.6.3.3
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (symlink to, text alongside). extracted text of PDF page 129 (printed p. 105) shows sec. 4.3.2.6 'Other Phonological Developments in Larantuka Malay' opening exactly with: 'Since Larantuka Malay did not lose schwa sounds as did other contact varieties of Malay in eastern Indonesia, phonemic stress has not developed. Stress is regular, and is found on the penultimate syllable (Kumanireng 1993: 66).' -- verbatim as quoted; the same paragraph recurs word for word under App. A.6.3.3 (the text layer24299ff). Surrounding context read: 4.3.2.4 gives the schwa-loss > final-stress minimal pairs (ba'rat/'barat) for the OTHER eastern varieties; 4.3.2.5 (Kumanireng 1993:54) says Larantuka…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the word; unlike the schwa-less eastern Malay varieties (where *schwa loss produced final-stressed minimal pairs), Larantuka Malay kept schwa and has no phonemic stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated: no schwa-conditioned shift to the final syllable is mentioned (contrast Kupang/Manado/North Moluccan Malay); Kaland 2025 Table 2.1 likewise lists Larantuka as 'P' with alternation 'n.a.'. Schwa is said to occur mostly in pre-penultimate syllables and never word-finally (Kumanireng 1993:54 via Paauw p. 104), so penultimate-schwa cases are rare but not addressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a phonology overview; no discussion of phrase-level prominence or citation forms. The claim is credited to Kumanireng 1993:66 (unpublished UI dissertation); Paauw did fieldwork in Larantuka but gives no independent stress evidence, and no acoustic study exists (Kaland 2025:15).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Malay of Larantuka town itself (Steinhauer 1991 explicitly excludes the Konga and Wure sub-dialects for lack of data; Paauw's fieldwork was in Larantuka). The deciding sentence in Paauw 2008 is explicitly credited to Kumanireng 1993:66 (unpublished Universitas Indonesia dissertation, the only full grammar); Paauw did his own Larantuka fieldwork (2003/2007, texts 13-17 in his appendix) but offers no independent stress analysis, and Kaland 2025 confirms no acoustic study of Larantuka Malay stress exists. Note the statement gives no schwa exception (unlike Kupang/Manado/North Moluccan Malay, where a penultimate schwa shifts stress to the final); Larantuka Malay retains phonemic schwa, mostly in pre-penultimate syllables (Kumanireng 1993:54 via Paauw p. 104).

sources.note: The thesis describes the phonological, lexical and morphological structure of Larantuka Malay and Palembang Malay synchronically and compares them diachronically (retentions, shared and particular innovations); the one phonological finding named is segmental (deletion of word-final consonants, ML called a 'vocalic' Malay enclave). The abstract says nothing about stress, tone or intonation; whether the fonologi chapter has a suprasegmental statement is unverified.
